questions.question: A clickstream Kinesis data stream already feeds several consumer applications that read from the same shards. A new fraud-scoring consumer must not compete with the existing consumers for read throughput. The team does not want to keep a second copy of the clickstream data. How should the new consumer read the data?
options: Register the fraud-scoring application as an enhanced fan-out consumer of the existing clickstream data stream.
Add the fraud-scoring application as another standard iterator consumer polling the existing clickstream shards.
Attach an Amazon Data Firehose stream that copies the records to Amazon S3 for the scorer to read.
Have the producers write every record to a second data stream reserved for the fraud-scoring application.
questions.correct_rationale: Enhanced fan-out gives the consumer dedicated throughput on the same stream, so nothing is duplicated.
distractor_rationales: A standard iterator consumer reads the same stream but shares shard throughput with the other consumers.
Firehose is another consumer of the stream and also writes a second copy of the data to S3.
A second stream gives isolated throughput but keeps a duplicate copy of every record.
questions.distractor_summary: WA isolates throughput by duplicating data; WB keeps one stream but shares throughput; X duplicates data and shares throughput.

questions.question: A Lambda function processes batches from a Kinesis data stream through an event source mapping. A single malformed record sometimes makes a whole batch fail and retry repeatedly. Records from invocations that still fail must be kept somewhere for later inspection. Which event source mapping configuration meets both needs?
options: Add an Amazon SQS queue as the on-failure destination and keep the full batch size unchanged.
Raise the function timeout and memory so that each large batch has more time to finish processing.
Turn on BisectBatchOnFunctionError and add an on-failure destination to the event source mapping.
Enable batch bisection on function errors so the mapping splits each failing batch into smaller halves.
questions.correct_rationale: Bisection isolates the bad record and the on-failure destination keeps details of records that still fail.
distractor_rationales: The destination retains failures, but whole batches still fail together because nothing isolates the bad record.
More time and memory do not help a batch that fails because of malformed data, and nothing is retained.
Bisection isolates the bad record, but nothing retains the records that keep failing.
questions.distractor_summary: WA isolates bad records without retention; WB retains failures without isolation; X addresses neither.

questions.question: Several applications and admin tools write order items to an Amazon DynamoDB table. A Lambda function must react to each insert, update, and delete as it happens. Changes made by every writer, including tools outside the main application, must be captured. Which design meets these requirements?
options: Enable DynamoDB Streams on the table and add a Lambda trigger that processes the stream records.
Export the table to Amazon S3 each night and have the function compare it with the previous export.
Add a global secondary index on a last-updated attribute and have the function read that index.
Change the main order application to invoke the Lambda function directly after each successful table write.
questions.correct_rationale: The stream records every modification regardless of writer, and the trigger invokes the function as changes occur.
distractor_rationales: A nightly export comparison sees every writer's changes but reacts a day late.
Reading an index is neither event-driven nor a reliable record of deletes.
The application call reacts immediately but misses changes made by other writers and admin tools.
questions.distractor_summary: WA is immediate but misses other writers; WB catches every writer but is a nightly batch; X is neither.

questions.question: A company must copy records from a supported SaaS application into Amazon S3 on a schedule without writing extraction code. The transfer must stay on AWS infrastructure instead of crossing the public internet. Which approach fits?
options: Use an AWS Transfer Family SFTP server that receives exported files from the SaaS application nightly.
Use Amazon Data Firehose with a direct PUT source that the SaaS application calls on a schedule.
Use an AWS DMS replication task with the SaaS application configured as the source endpoint.
Use an Amazon AppFlow flow on a schedule with AWS PrivateLink enabled for the SaaS connection.
questions.correct_rationale: AppFlow runs scheduled flows from SaaS sources without code and supports PrivateLink for private transfer.
distractor_rationales: SFTP needs the SaaS side to export and push files, which is custom work outside AWS infrastructure.
Firehose direct PUT needs the SaaS side to push data with custom integration, over public endpoints.
DMS migrates databases; it does not treat SaaS applications as source endpoints.
questions.distractor_summary: Only AppFlow combines code-free scheduled SaaS flows with PrivateLink; the others need custom integration.

questions.question: A Kinesis data stream feeds a consumer whose logic sometimes needs a bug fix followed by reprocessing. After future fixes, the team must be able to replay records from several days back. Replays must read from the same stream rather than from a separate archive copy, and the stream's retention period is shorter than that window. What should the team do now?
options: Increase the stream's data retention period so the consumer can restart from an earlier timestamp.
Archive the stream to Amazon S3 with Data Firehose and reprocess the archived objects after each fix.
Plan to restart the consumer at the oldest available record and leave the stream settings unchanged.
Turn on enhanced fan-out for the consumer so it can read faster and catch up on missed records.
questions.correct_rationale: A longer retention period keeps several days of records in the stream itself for a timestamp-based replay.
distractor_rationales: An S3 archive allows replay from days back, but it reads a separate copy instead of the stream.
Restarting at the oldest record reads the same stream but cannot reach back further than the short retention.
Faster reads do not keep records any longer, so older records stay unavailable.
questions.distractor_summary: WA reaches back via a separate archive; WB uses the stream but its short retention; X changes read speed, not retention.

questions.question: A nightly AWS Glue Spark job reads new JSON files from an S3 prefix that receives thousands of small files. Each run must skip the files that earlier runs already processed. The job must cut the overhead of opening many small input files in separate tasks. Which configuration meets both needs?
options: Set groupFiles and groupSize in the table parameters while reading the full prefix on every run.
Enable job bookmarks on the job and set file grouping parameters on the source table.
Enable AWS Glue job bookmarks so that each run picks up data that earlier runs did not read.
Increase the number of workers so each small file gets its own executor and finishes sooner.
questions.correct_rationale: Job bookmarks prevent reprocessing of files earlier runs read, and groupFiles in the table parameters lets each task read many small JSON files into one in-memory partition; JSON is a supported DynamicFrame format for grouping.
distractor_rationales: Grouping reduces small-file overhead, but every run rereads files that were already processed.
Bookmarks stop reprocessing, but each small file is still opened in its own task.
More workers add cost and still reprocess old files while keeping per-file overhead.
questions.distractor_summary: WA stops reprocessing only partly; WB groups files but rereads all data; X addresses neither.

distractor_rationales: Gzip CSV is still row-based and the Batch Operations job is extra infrastructure.

A view is SQL in Athena but leaves the data in CSV.

Add automatic scaling to a task instance group using a CloudWatch metric like available YARN memory.
Have an operator add task nodes by hand before month-end and remove them after processing completes.
Configure automatic scaling on the core instance group so core nodes grow and shrink with demand.
questions.correct_rationale: Task nodes do not store HDFS data, and an automatic scaling policy adds and removes them on a CloudWatch metric.
distractor_rationales: Primary and core purchasing options cannot be changed on a running cluster; a new cluster is required.
Task nodes avoid HDFS risk, but manual changes are not automatic.
Core nodes scale automatically here but store HDFS data, so removing them risks data.

Run the jobs on a long-running Amazon EMR on EC2 cluster with a fixed number of core nodes.

Run the jobs on Amazon EMR on EKS with node groups that the team itself manages and patches.

Deploy the DAGs to an Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow environment and let AWS operate it.

questions.question: Partner files arrive in an S3 bucket throughout the day, and an AWS Glue workflow processes them. The workflow must be started by the arrival events instead of a fixed schedule. Each run should wait to collect a set number of events or a time window rather than starting for every file. How should the workflow be started?
options: Invoke a Lambda function from each S3 PUT notification that calls StartWorkflowRun for that one object.
Use an S3 Lifecycle rule to move arriving objects to another prefix that a Glue crawler reads later.
Start the workflow from an EventBridge event trigger configured with a batch size and a batch window.
Run the workflow from a scheduled trigger every few hours that processes the files that have accumulated.

distractor_rationales: Per-object Lambda calls are event-driven but start one run for each file.
Lifecycle rules manage storage classes and expiration; they do not start workflows.
A scheduled trigger batches files but is time-driven rather than started by events.

questions.question: An AWS Glue workflow runs an ETL job that writes new partitions to Amazon S3. A crawler must update the Data Catalog right after the job finishes successfully. options: Create an EventBridge rule on the Glue job state change event that starts the crawler from outside.
Have an analyst start the crawler from the console after confirming the job output each morning.
Add a conditional trigger in the workflow that starts the crawler when the ETL job succeeds.
Add a scheduled trigger inside the workflow that starts the crawler at a fixed hour each night.
questions.correct_rationale: A conditional trigger inside the workflow fires on job success and starts the crawler.
distractor_rationales: The EventBridge rule reacts to job completion but keeps the dependency outside the workflow.
A manual start is neither immediate nor defined in the workflow.
A scheduled trigger lives in the workflow but does not wait for the job to succeed.

questions.question: During a migration, a team must start an AWS Glue job and manage its future runs from one scheduling service. One run must happen a single time at a specific future date and time. Another run of a cleanup job is needed every weekday morning. Which approach handles both runs?
options: Create a one-time schedule and a cron-based recurring schedule in Amazon EventBridge Scheduler.
Use an AWS Step Functions Wait state that pauses until the planned timestamp and then starts the Glue job.
Create an S3 event notification that starts the job when the migration team uploads a marker file.
Create an EventBridge rule with a cron expression that runs a job every weekday morning.
questions.correct_rationale: Scheduler supports both one-time invocations and recurring cron schedules in one service.
distractor_rationales: A Wait state can start one run at the planned timestamp but does not provide the weekday schedule.
An upload-driven event depends on someone uploading a file and covers neither schedule.
A cron rule covers the weekday runs but not a single run at one future date.

questions.question: A pipeline must apply the same Lambda transformation to millions of objects in an S3 bucket. The work must run with high parallelism. The status and failures of each object's processing must be visible in workflow execution history. Which design fits?
options: Loop through the objects one by one in a state machine with a Choice state and a counter.
Run one AWS Glue Python shell job that downloads and transforms each object in sequence.
Have one Lambda function list the bucket and fire asynchronous invocations of the transform per object.
Use a Step Functions Map state in Distributed mode that reads the object list from Amazon S3.
questions.correct_rationale: Distributed mode runs large-scale parallel child workflows whose results are tracked in execution history.
distractor_rationales: A Choice loop records each step in history but runs sequentially.
A sequential Python shell job is neither parallel nor tracked per object in a workflow.
Asynchronous fan-out is parallel but leaves no workflow history of each object's outcome.

questions.question: A Lambda function loads records into an Amazon RDS database, and traffic spikes open too many database connections. Concurrent executions of this function must be capped to protect the database. The function must keep its existing event source without adding a queue in front of it. What should the team configure?
options: Raise the function's memory setting so each invocation finishes sooner and releases its connection earlier.
Switch the database writes to asynchronous invocations with an on-failure destination for any errors.
Route invocations through a new Amazon SQS queue and set maximum concurrency on its event source mapping.
Set reserved concurrency on the function to a level the database connection pool can absorb.
questions.correct_rationale: Reserved concurrency caps the function's concurrent executions without changing its event source.
distractor_rationales: More memory keeps the event source but does not cap concurrent executions during spikes.
Asynchronous invocation with a destination neither caps concurrency nor keeps the source unchanged.
Maximum concurrency on an SQS mapping caps concurrency but adds a queue.
questions.distractor_summary: WA caps via a new queue; WB keeps the source with no cap; X neither.

questions.question: An API backed by a Lambda function that queries a data mart shows latency spikes caused by initialization when traffic rises each morning. Which configuration addresses the initialization delay?

Increase the function timeout so requests that wait for initialization do not end in errors.
Add an on-failure destination to the function so slow invocations are sent to a queue.
Configure provisioned concurrency so pre-initialized execution environments are ready each morning.
questions.correct_rationale: Provisioned concurrency keeps environments initialized before requests arrive.
distractor_rationales: Reserved concurrency guarantees and caps capacity but does not pre-initialize environments.
A longer timeout hides errors but keeps the initialization delay.
Destinations handle invocation results; they do not remove initialization time.

Keep the standard iterator event source mapping and increase the batch size of each function read.
Register a dedicated enhanced fan-out consumer and point the function's event source mapping at it.
Copy the stream to Amazon S3 with Data Firehose and trigger the function from S3 object events.

Keep the history in S3 and have analysts query it with Amazon Athena outside the Redshift clusters.
Export the history to an Amazon DynamoDB table and read it from each cluster through an API layer.
Run COPY commands that load the clickstream history into local tables on each of the two clusters.

COPY allows joins with local tables but loads a copy into each cluster.

Load order status into Redshift each night with an AWS Glue job and join it in the reports.
Point the BI tool at the PostgreSQL database directly so the dashboards read live status from the source.
Unload warehouse tables to S3 and query them together with PostgreSQL exports in Amazon Athena.

Store the tables in Apache Iceberg format in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and query them with Athena.

Store the tables in JSON Lines format and use Athena views to hide records marked as deleted.

questions.question: A security review must find any S3 buckets or IAM roles in the data accounts that are shared outside the organization. Findings must come from analysis of the resource-based policies, not from waiting for access to happen. The review must not depend on engineers reading each policy by hand. Which tool should the team use?
options: Search CloudTrail logs for requests from outside accounts and list the buckets and roles they used.
Have engineers read every bucket policy and role trust policy by hand and list the external principals.
Create an IAM Access Analyzer external access analyzer for the organization and review its findings.
Turn on S3 server access logs and check by hand each week which outside accounts made requests.
questions.correct_rationale: Access Analyzer reasons over resource-based policies to report external sharing without manual review.
distractor_rationales: CloudTrail searches are automated, but they find sharing after access happens.
Reading policies analyzes them, but it is the manual review the team wants to avoid.
Access logs show past requests and need manual weekly checks.
questions.distractor_summary: WA is automated but needs access to happen; WB analyzes policies by hand; X waits for requests and is manual.

questions.question: A compliance standard requires that regulated data in an S3 bucket be protected by two layers of encryption. Both encryption layers must be applied by Amazon S3 on the server side when objects are uploaded. The keys must be managed in AWS KMS so key use is logged in CloudTrail. Which encryption setting should the bucket require?
options: Require SSE-S3 on the bucket and also turn on S3 Bucket Keys to add a second layer of protection.
Require SSE-KMS on the bucket and also encrypt each file in the client before it is uploaded.
Require dual-layer server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys (DSSE-KMS) on uploads to the bucket.
Require SSE-S3 on the bucket and rely on TLS during upload as the second layer of encryption.
questions.correct_rationale: DSSE-KMS applies two server-side encryption layers with KMS keys whose use is logged.
distractor_rationales: SSE-S3 is server side, but its keys are not KMS keys, and Bucket Keys do not add a layer.
This gives two layers with KMS keys, but one layer is applied in the client, not by S3.
TLS protects transit, not storage, and SSE-S3 does not use KMS keys.
questions.distractor_summary: WA uses KMS but one layer is client side; WB is server side without KMS; X has one storage layer without KMS.

questions.question: An application stores customer records in Amazon DynamoDB, and a few attributes hold sensitive tax numbers. The tax numbers must be encrypted before they leave the application, so DynamoDB does not see plaintext. Other attributes must stay readable for queries, so encryption must work at the attribute level. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Turn on DynamoDB encryption at rest with a customer managed KMS key for the customer table.
Encrypt the whole item in the application with a KMS key and store it as one binary attribute.
Use the AWS Database Encryption SDK in the app to encrypt the tax number attributes client side.
Turn on DynamoDB encryption at rest with an AWS owned key and mask tax numbers in reports later.
questions.correct_rationale: The SDK encrypts chosen attributes in the client, so DynamoDB does not see them and others stay readable.
distractor_rationales: Encryption at rest keeps attributes queryable, but DynamoDB still receives the plaintext.
Whole-item encryption happens in the client, but no attribute stays readable for queries.
At-rest encryption with an AWS owned key still sends plaintext, and masking later does not help.
questions.distractor_summary: WA encrypts client side but the whole item; WB keeps attributes readable but encrypts server side; X is server side with masking.

questions.question: A company runs data workloads in many member accounts of AWS Organizations, and new accounts are added each quarter. API activity in every account, including accounts added later, must be logged for audit. The logging must be set up once centrally, not configured in each member account. How should audit logging be set up?
options: Ask each account owner to review the CloudTrail event history in the console when audits start.
Create a trail in the management account that logs events for the management account alone.
Create an organization trail from the management account that logs events for all member accounts.
Create a trail in each member account by hand and add a step to the checklist for new accounts.
questions.correct_rationale: An organization trail is set up once and covers all member accounts, including new ones.
distractor_rationales: Event history is per account, short-lived, and needs each owner to review it.
A management-account trail is central, but it does not log member account activity.
Per-account trails log every account, but each one is set up separately in that account.
questions.distractor_summary: WA covers all accounts but per account; WB is central but misses members; X is per account and incomplete.

questions.question: Auditors want a record of the requests made to a raw-data bucket, including the requester, operation, and object key. The record must cover the requests made to the bucket's objects, not just changes to the bucket configuration. The records must be delivered by S3 to a log bucket without a custom logging application. What should the data engineer turn on?
options: Write a proxy application that receives all bucket requests and writes its own request log files.
Turn on S3 server access logging for the raw-data bucket with delivery to a separate log bucket.
Turn on S3 Inventory reports for the bucket and deliver them each day to a separate log bucket.
Rely on the CloudTrail management events that record changes to the bucket configuration settings.
questions.correct_rationale: Server access logs record each request to the bucket and S3 delivers them to a log bucket.
distractor_rationales: The proxy logs object requests, but it is the custom logging application the team wants to avoid.
Inventory lists objects and is delivered by S3, but it records no requests at all.
Management events need no custom code, but they cover configuration changes, not object requests.
questions.distractor_summary: WA logs requests with custom code; WB is S3-delivered but config-scoped; X is S3-delivered with no requests.

questions.question: A company has thousands of S3 buckets across its accounts and does not know where personal data is stored. The team needs broad, ongoing visibility into which buckets likely hold sensitive data. The team does not want to pay to scan every object in every bucket. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Turn on Macie automated sensitive data discovery to sample a set of objects in each bucket.
Run one Macie discovery job on a single bucket picked at random and use it as a guide for the rest.
Ask bucket owners to fill in a yearly survey that lists any personal data their buckets hold.
Create Macie sensitive data discovery jobs that scan every object in all buckets each night in full.
questions.correct_rationale: Automated discovery evaluates the whole estate on an ongoing basis by sampling objects instead of scanning all.
distractor_rationales: One random bucket keeps scanning small, but it does not give broad visibility across buckets.
A yearly survey is neither ongoing nor based on scanning the data.
Nightly full jobs give broad visibility, but they scan every object, which the team wants to avoid.
questions.distractor_summary: WA is broad but scans everything; WB is cheap but narrow; X is neither ongoing nor data-based.

lessons.title: Reading two constraints in an ingestion question
body: Most ingestion questions give you a working pipeline and two extra conditions. Find each condition and ask which part of the design it rules out. A Kinesis consumer that must not compete with existing readers needs dedicated read throughput, and a refusal to keep a second copy rules out a duplicate stream, which leaves an enhanced fan-out consumer on the existing stream.

Lambda event source mappings work the same way. A single malformed record that fails a whole batch points to BisectBatchOnFunctionError, which splits the failed batch to isolate bad records. A separate need to keep records that still fail points to an on-failure destination. An answer that covers one condition and not the other is the typical distractor.

For Spark and Hadoop work, separate who runs the infrastructure from how capacity changes. EMR Serverless acquires resources for each job and releases them when the job ends, while on an EMR cluster the guidance is to keep core nodes small and vary task nodes. Glue job bookmarks keep state so reruns do not reprocess old data, and an Athena CTAS query can write a table's data as Parquet using SQL alone.

lessons.title: Choosing where data lives and how it is found
body: Start a store question with the access pattern, then check how fresh the data must be and whether copies are allowed. Several Redshift clusters querying one S3 dataset without loading it point to Redshift Spectrum. Live operational rows joined into reporting point to federated queries. Record-level updates and time travel on S3 data point to Apache Iceberg tables queried from Athena.

Catalog questions usually come down to cost and freshness. With partition projection, Athena calculates partition values and locations from table properties that you configure on the table in AWS Glue. A Glue crawler that uses S3 event notifications lists the objects from those events instead of every object in the path.

Lifecycle and modelling questions test which mechanism does the work and what it costs. S3 Lifecycle rules apply to existing objects as well as new ones, and DynamoDB TTL deletes expired items without consuming write throughput. Distributing two Redshift tables on their joining keys collocates matching rows on the same slices, and a DynamoDB global secondary index serves queries on non-key attributes.

lessons.title: Operating pipelines: automation, cost control, and evidence
body: Operations questions reward the managed feature that does the job with no extra code. S3 events delivered to EventBridge can be routed by rules to several targets, and Redshift materialized views can refresh automatically when their base tables change. DataBrew recipes save transformation steps that can be reused on other datasets.

When a question mentions runaway query spend, look for a control scoped to the right group. An Athena per-query data usage control on a workgroup cancels queries in that workgroup that exceed the limit. A QuickSight dataset imported into SPICE is reused without querying the source again, which takes load off the source system.

For troubleshooting, decide where the evidence already lives. CloudWatch Logs Insights searches and analyzes log data interactively, and Glue publishes job metrics to CloudWatch, where you can alarm on them. Data quality rules belong in the pipeline: Glue Data Quality defines rules in DQDL, and in DataBrew a ruleset fails validation if any criterion of a rule is not met, so a step can stop a load on one failed check.

lessons.title: Access, encryption, audit, and privacy for data engineers
body: Credential and network questions separate storing a secret from rotating it. Secrets Manager can rotate secrets on an automatic schedule, so jobs read the secret at runtime instead of embedding it. For authorization at scale, Lake Formation tag-based access control grants access when the principal's tag value matches the resource's, and Redshift data sharing gives consumers read-only access to live data without copying it.

Encryption across accounts needs permission in two places. A KMS key used by another account must allow that use in the key policy, and the external account must also grant it in an IAM policy. For column-level privacy inside Redshift, dynamic data masking applies obfuscation rules to a user or role at query time, so one table can serve roles with different views.

Audit questions ask you to capture exactly the events that matter. CloudTrail advanced event selectors can filter data events, for example to log only DeleteObject calls on a bucket, and Logs Insights can then query the log group that receives them. To find sensitive data across a large S3 estate, Macie automated sensitive data discovery shows where it might reside.
